In 1911, someone stole the Mona Lisa, and it took the Louvre more than a day to even notice.
The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, a handyman who had worked at the museum, building glass cases for its paintings.
On a Sunday, he hid inside a storage closet, and waited all night.
Monday morning, the museum was closed. He put on the white smock every worker wore, and walked straight up to the painting.
He lifted it off the wall,
took it out of its frame in a stairwell,
and hid it under his smock.
The door was locked, so a plumber helpfully opened it for him.
The next day, a painter came to sketch the Mona Lisa, and found four empty hooks.
The guards assumed it was just being photographed.
When they finally realized, the Louvre shut down for a week. Police even questioned Pablo Picasso.
And when it reopened, crowds lined up just to stare at the empty space on the wall.
Newspapers everywhere printed her face. The Mona Lisa had been well known. Now, she was famous.
For two years, she sat in a trunk in Peruggia's apartment.
Then he took her to Florence and tried to sell her to an art dealer, who called the police.
Peruggia said he just wanted to bring her home to Italy.
He spent a few months in jail. And the painting he stole became the most famous in the world.
